blocks.body: Sewer rodding clears a blocked main line with a long, flexible steel cable fed through a cleanout access point. A cutting head on the end breaks through roots, grease, and debris and pushes the blockage toward the street connection, restoring flow through the pipe. It's the standard first fix for a clogged or backed-up sewer line. For most homes, it's the only fix needed.

blocks.h2: Rodding a Line Several Units Share
blocks.body: In a Ravenswood two-flat or three-flat, every kitchen, bath and laundry eventually drains into one lateral. When it clogs, the garden unit floods first and everyone upstairs loses the use of their drains until it's cleared. We ask the other units to stop running water while we work, clear the line to the city main and run the camera so the owner can see whether roots, grease or a break caused it. Then the building can plan the next step together.

items.q: How often should an old Ravenswood line be rodded?
items.preview: Yearly if roots are a problem.
items.answer: If roots have blocked it before, once a year is common, ideally in late winter.

items.q: Can you rod a line with no cleanout?
items.preview: Usually, or we can add one.
items.answer: Usually through a toilet or vent. Adding a cleanout makes future service much easier.
Yes, with a cutter sized for the pipe. The camera afterward shows its condition.

items.q: Who should call when a two-flat backs up?
items.preview: The owner, or whoever manages the building.
items.answer: The building owner. We'll clear the shared line and show everyone what caused it.

items.q: Will you need access to every unit?
items.answer: Usually not. We work from the basement or an outside cleanout.
